title: 2 Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry
text:
What is meant by the relative atomic mass of an element?


AThe mass of one atom compared with the mass of one electron


BThe weighted mean mass of an atom compared with \(\frac{1}{12}\) of the mass of a carbon-12 atom


CThe mass of one hydrogen atom compared with one carbon atom


DThe mass of one proton compared with one neutron



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean because naturally occurring elements may contain several isotopes.







Which statement correctly describes two isotopes of the same element?


AThey have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.


BThey have different numbers of protons but the same number of neutrons.


CThey have different numbers of protons and different chemical properties.


DThey have the same mass number and different atomic numbers.



Check answer





Show explanation


A. Isotopes have the same proton number, so they are the same element, but different neutron numbers.







What is the relative formula mass of \((\ce{NH4})2\ce{SO4}\)? Use \(A_r\): N = 14.0, H = 1.0, S = 32.1 and O = 16.0.


A98.1


B98.0


C132.1


D132.0



Check answer





Show explanation


C. \(M_r=(2\times14.0)+(8\times1.0)+32.1+(4\times16.0)=132.1\).







An element contains 91.75% of an isotope with mass 55.0 and 8.25% of an isotope with mass 56.0. What is its relative atomic mass?


A55.000


B55.500


C56.000


D55.083



Check answer





Show explanation


D. \(A_r=(55.0\times0.9175)+(56.0\times0.0825)=55.0825\), which rounds to 55.083.







What is the number of molecules in \(500\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of oxygen gas at RTP? Take the molar gas volume as \(24.0\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}\).


A\(3.00\times10^{23}\)


B\(3.00\times10^{26}\)


C\(1.25\times10^{21}\)


D\(1.25\times10^{22}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


D. \(500\ \mathrm{cm^3}=0.500\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), so \(n=0.500/24.0=0.0208\ \mathrm{mol}\) and \(N=0.0208\times6.02\times10^{23}=1.25\times10^{22}\).







Which set of coefficients balances the equation?
\[\ce{Mg3N2 + H2O -> Mg(OH)2 + NH3}\]


A\(1,6,3,2\)


B\(1,3,3,2\)


C\(2,6,3,4\)


D\(1,4,3,2\)



Check answer





Show explanation


A. Three magnesium atoms require \(3\ce{Mg(OH)2}\); two nitrogen atoms give \(2\ce{NH3}\), requiring six water molecules.










A hydrated carbonate has formula \(\ce{X2CO3.10H2O}\) and relative formula mass 286. What is element X? Use \(A_r\): C = 12.0, O = 16.0 and H = 1.0.


ALi


BK


CNa


DRb



Check answer





Show explanation


C. The anhydrous part contributes \(12+48=60\) and the water contributes \(180\), so \(2A_r(X)=286-240=46\) and \(A_r(X)=23\).







Nitrogen reacts with excess hydrogen. \(2.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) of nitrogen is available at standard conditions and 15.0% reacts. What mass of ammonia forms? Use a molar gas volume of \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3\ mol^{-1}}\) for this question.
\[\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}\]


A\(2.83\ \mathrm{g}\)


B\(1.42\ \mathrm{g}\)


C\(0.455\ \mathrm{g}\)


D\(0.213\ \mathrm{g}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Reacted nitrogen is \(2.00\times0.150/22.4=0.0134\ \mathrm{mol}\); ammonia is \(0.0268\ \mathrm{mol}\), giving approximately \(0.455\ \mathrm{g}\).







Chlorine reacts with cold aqueous sodium hydroxide:
\[\ce{Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O}\]
What mass of \(\ce{NaOCl}\) forms from \(0.125\ \mathrm{mol}\) of \(\ce{Cl2}\) with excess \(\ce{NaOH}\)? Use \(M_r(\ce{NaOCl})=74.5\).


A\(13.3\ \mathrm{g}\)


B\(9.31\ \mathrm{g}\)


C\(18.6\ \mathrm{g}\)


D\(26.6\ \mathrm{g}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. The mole ratio is \(1:1\), so \(n(\ce{NaOCl})=0.125\) and mass \(=0.125\times74.5=9.31\ \mathrm{g}\).







When \(7.40\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\ce{Mg(NO3)2}\) is heated, what mass of nitrogen dioxide forms? Use \(M_r(\ce{Mg(NO3)2})=148\).


A\(4.60\ \mathrm{g}\)


B\(1.50\ \mathrm{g}\)


C\(2.30\ \mathrm{g}\)


D\(3.00\ \mathrm{g}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


A. \(7.40/148=0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\) of salt forms \(0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\) of \(\ce{NO2}\), so the mass is \(0.100\times46.0=4.60\ \mathrm{g}\).







A \(0.144\ \mathrm{g}\) aluminium compound burns to form \(72.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(\ce{CO2}\) at RTP. Which is its formula? Use \(A_r(\ce{Al})=27.0\).


A\(\ce{Al2C3}\)


B\(\ce{Al3C4}\)


C\(\ce{Al5C3}\)


D\(\ce{Al4C3}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


D. \(n(\ce{CO2})=0.0720/24.0=0.00300\ \mathrm{mol}\), so the sample contains \(0.00300\ \mathrm{mol}\) C. The aluminium-to-carbon ratio is \(0.00533:0.00300\approx4:3\).







What metal reacts completely with \(1.15\ \mathrm{g}\) of metal and \(300\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of oxygen at RTP to form an oxide containing \(\ce{O^{2-}}\)? Choose from Ca, Na, K and Mg.


ACa


BNa


CK


DMg



Check answer





Show explanation


D. \(n(\ce{O2})=0.300/24.0=0.0125\ \mathrm{mol}\). For magnesium, \(1.15/24.3=0.0473\ \mathrm{mol}\) and the required oxygen is \(0.0237\ \mathrm{mol}\), so oxygen is available in the expected limiting ratio.







A coin has mass \(10.0\ \mathrm{g}\) and contains 20.0% nickel by mass. How many nickel atoms are present? Use \(A_r(\ce{Ni})=58.7\).


A\(4.30\times10^{22}\)


B\(1.03\times10^{23}\)


C\(1.20\times10^{24}\)


D\(2.05\times10^{22}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


D. Nickel mass is \(2.00\ \mathrm{g}\), so \(n=2.00/58.7=0.0341\ \mathrm{mol}\) and \(N=2.05\times10^{22}\) atoms.










Carbon is burned in a limited amount of oxygen. Half the carbon forms \(\ce{CO2}\) and half forms \(\ce{CO}\). The carbon oxides are passed through excess aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which gas volume remains if the starting carbon sample is \(1.00\ \mathrm{g}\) and the gas volume is measured at RTP?


A\(3.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)


B\(2.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)


C\(1.50\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)


D\(1.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


D. The amount of carbon monoxide is \(0.5/12.0=0.0417\ \mathrm{mol}\), so the remaining gas volume is \(0.0417\times24.0=1.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).







An eggshell is 5.0% \(\ce{CaCO3}\) by mass. Each egg contains a \(50.0\ \mathrm{g}\) shell, and the carbonate in the shell neutralises \(50.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) ethanoic acid. How many eggshells are needed?
\[\ce{CaCO3 + 2CH3COOH -> Ca(CH3COO)2 + H2O + CO2}\]


A4


B3


C2


D1



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Acid amount is \(0.0500\times2.00=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\), requiring \(0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\) carbonate, or \(5.00\ \mathrm{g}\). Each shell contains \(2.50\ \mathrm{g}\), so two shells are required.







An oxide sample is dissolved in \(250\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of solution. A \(25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) portion requires \(15.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) sulfuric acid. If the oxide is \(\ce{K2O}\), what mass was present?
\[\ce{K2O + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + H2O}\]


A\(56.6\ \mathrm{g}\)


B\(47.1\ \mathrm{g}\)


C\(28.3\ \mathrm{g}\)


D\(2.83\ \mathrm{g}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


C. The aliquot contains \(0.0150\times2.00=0.0300\ \mathrm{mol}\) acid; the whole solution contains \(0.300\ \mathrm{mol}\), hence \(0.300\ \mathrm{mol}\) \(\ce{K2O}\) and mass \(0.300\times94.2=28.3\ \mathrm{g}\).







In a ferrochrome sample, \(1.00\ \mathrm{g}\) requires \(13.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(0.100\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) \(\ce{K2Cr2O7}\). The chromium(VI) reagent oxidises iron(II) according to a \(1:6\) mole ratio. What percentage by mass of the sample is iron?


A43.9%


B12.2%


C4.39%


D1.22%



Check answer





Show explanation


A. Dichromate amount is \(0.0131\times0.100=0.00131\ \mathrm{mol}\); iron amount is \(6\times0.00131=0.00786\ \mathrm{mol}\). Its mass is \(0.00786\times55.8=0.439\ \mathrm{g}\), or 43.9%.







Equal volumes of methane and ethane are sparked with excess oxygen. The carbon dioxide is removed by aqueous potassium hydroxide. What fraction of the original hydrocarbon volume is absorbed?


A45%


B150%


C100%


D50%



Check answer





Show explanation


B. One volume methane gives one volume carbon dioxide; one volume ethane gives two. Thus two starting volumes produce three volumes absorbed, i.e. 150% of the hydrocarbon volume.







In acid solution, \(\ce{Sn^{2+}}\) reduces \(\ce{MnO4^-}\) to \(\ce{Mn^{2+}}\). What amount of \(\ce{Mn^{2+}}\) can form from \(9.50\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\ce{SnCl2}\)? Take \(M_r(\ce{SnCl2})=190\) and use the ratio \(5\ce{Sn^{2+}}:2\ce{MnO4^-}\).


A\(0.010\ \mathrm{mol}\)


B\(0.020\ \mathrm{mol}\)


C\(0.050\ \mathrm{mol}\)


D\(0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. \(9.50/190=0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\) \(\ce{Sn^{2+}}\). The ratio gives \(n(\ce{MnO4^-})=0.0200\ \mathrm{mol}\) and hence \(0.0200\ \mathrm{mol}\) \(\ce{Mn^{2+}}\).







For the balanced reaction below, what volume of nitrogen forms at RTP when \(0.783\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\ce{Ba(NO3)2}\) reacts? Use \(M_r(\ce{Ba(NO3)2})=261\).
\[\ce{10Al + 3Ba(NO3)2 -> 3BaO + 5Al2O3 + 3N2}\]


A\(144\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)


B\(93.6\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)


C\(72.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)


D\(1.62\ \mathrm{cm^3}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


C. \(n(\ce{Ba(NO3)2})=0.783/261=0.00300\ \mathrm{mol}\), and the equation gives the same amount of \(\ce{N2}\); \(V=0.00300\times24.0=0.0720\ \mathrm{dm^3}=72.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\).

title: 2 Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry
text:
(a) Define relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass. [2 marks]
(b) State what the symbols \(A_r\) and \(M_r\) represent. Explain the difference between relative molecular mass and relative formula mass. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the relative formula mass of \(\ce{MgO}\), \(\ce{H2SO4}\), \((\ce{NH4})3\ce{PO4}\) and \(\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}\). Use \(A_r\): H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0, P = 31.0, S = 32.1, Mg = 24.3, Cu = 63.5. [4 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Relative isotopic mass compares an isotope with \(\frac{1}{12}\) of a carbon-12 atom. Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of the isotopic masses of an element on the same scale.


(b) \(A_r\) is relative atomic mass and \(M_r\) is relative molecular or formula mass. A molecular mass refers to one molecule; a formula mass is used for an ionic lattice or giant structure.


(c) \(M_r(\ce{MgO})=40.3\); \(M_r(\ce{H2SO4})=98.1\); \(M_r((\ce{NH4})3\ce{PO4})=149.0\); \(M_r(\ce{CuSO4.5H2O})=249.5\).






(a) State the Avogadro constant and explain what one mole of a substance contains. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the number of molecules and the total number of atoms in \(1.00\ \mathrm{mol}\) of water. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the number of sodium ions, carbonate ions and total ions in \(1.00\ \mathrm{mol}\) of \(\ce{Na2CO3}\). [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(L=6.02\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\); one mole contains \(6.02\times10^{23}\) specified particles.


(b) \(6.02\times10^{23}\) water molecules. Each has three atoms, so total atoms \(=1.806\times10^{24}\).


(c) There are \(2\times6.02\times10^{23}=1.204\times10^{24}\) sodium ions and \(6.02\times10^{23}\) carbonate ions. Total ions \(=1.806\times10^{24}\).






A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 180.
(a) Determine its empirical formula. [3 marks]
(b) Determine its molecular formula. [2 marks]
(c) Explain why percentages can be treated as masses in a 100 g sample. [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) For 100 g: C \(=40.0/12.0=3.33\); H \(=6.7/1.0=6.70\); O \(=53.3/16.0=3.33\). Divide by 3.33 to obtain \(\ce{CH2O}\).


(b) Empirical formula mass \(=30.0\); multiplier \(=180/30.0=6\), so molecular formula \(\ce{C6H12O6}\).


(c) In a 100 g sample, each percentage has the same numerical value in grams.









Magnesium reacts with a mixture containing \(0.500\ \mathrm{g}\) of quartz sand, \(0.500\ \mathrm{g}\) of powdered silica and \(2.40\ \mathrm{g}\) of magnesium. The silica is represented by \(\ce{SiO2}\).
(a) Write an equation for the formation of magnesium oxide from silica and identify the limiting reagent using amounts in moles. [4 marks]
(b) Silicon magnesium, \(\ce{Mg2Si}\), reacts with hydrochloric acid to form silane, \(\ce{SiH4}\). Write the balanced equation and classify the reaction of silane with oxygen as combustion, redox or neutralisation. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the maximum mass of \(\ce{HSiCl3}\) formed if \(35.125\ \mathrm{g}\) of silicon reacts according to \(\ce{Si + 3HCl -> HSiCl3 + H2}\). [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(\ce{2Mg + SiO2 -> 2MgO + Si}\). \(n(\ce{Mg})=2.40/24.3=0.0988\ \mathrm{mol}\); \(n(\ce{SiO2})\) in the two samples is about \(0.0167\ \mathrm{mol}\). Magnesium is in excess for this equation; silica is limiting.


(b) \(\ce{Mg2Si + 4HCl -> 2MgCl2 + SiH4}\). Burning silane is a combustion reaction and also a redox reaction.


(c) \(n(\ce{Si})=35.125/28.1=1.25\ \mathrm{mol}\). The equation gives \(1.25\ \mathrm{mol}\) \(\ce{HSiCl3}\); mass \(=1.25\times135.5=169\ \mathrm{g}\).






A hydrated cobalt sulfate has formula \(\ce{CoSO4.xH2O}\) and relative formula mass 173.0. Use \(A_r\): Co = 59.0, S = 32.0, O = 16.0 and H = 1.0.
(a) Calculate the value of \(x\). [3 marks]
(b) A \(2.00\ \mathrm{g}\) sample of the hydrate is heated to constant mass. The residue is \(1.09\ \mathrm{g}\). Calculate the amount of water removed. [2 marks]
(c) State why heating is continued to constant mass. [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) The anhydrous part has mass \(59.0+32.0+64.0=155.0\). Water contributes \(18.0x=173.0-155.0=18.0\), so \(x=1\) and the formula is \(\ce{CoSO4.H2O}\).


(b) Water lost \(=0.91\ \mathrm{g}\); amount \(=0.91/18.0=0.0506\ \mathrm{mol}\).


(c) To ensure all water of crystallisation has been removed and the mass is no longer changing.






Hydrogen reacts with nitrogen:
\[\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}\]
(a) Calculate the amount of nitrogen in \(10.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) of nitrogen gas at RTP. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the volume of hydrogen needed for complete reaction with this nitrogen. [2 marks]
(c) A solution contains \(0.250\ \mathrm{mol}\) of ammonia in \(500\ \mathrm{cm^3}\). Calculate its concentration in \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\). [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(n=10.0/24.0=0.417\ \mathrm{mol}\).


(b) \(n(\ce{H2})=3\times0.417=1.25\ \mathrm{mol}\); volume \(=1.25\times24.0=30.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).


(c) \(500\ \mathrm{cm^3}=0.500\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), so \(c=0.250/0.500=0.500\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\).









A \(1.00\ \mathrm{g}\) sample of carbon reacts with a limited amount of oxygen. Half of the carbon forms \(\ce{CO2}\) and half forms \(\ce{CO}\).
(a) Write the two balanced equations for the reactions. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the total amount of oxygen atoms used. [2 marks]
(c) The mixture of carbon oxides is passed through excess sodium hydroxide solution. Calculate the volume of gas remaining at RTP. [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}\) and \(\ce{2C + O2 -> 2CO}\).


(b) Carbon amount is \(1.00/12.0=0.0833\ \mathrm{mol}\); half forms each oxide. Oxygen atoms used \(=0.0417\times2+0.0417\times1=0.125\ \mathrm{mol}\).


(c) Sodium hydroxide absorbs \(\ce{CO2}\) while \(\ce{CO}\) remains. The remaining amount is \(0.0417\ \mathrm{mol}\), so its volume is \(0.0417\times24.0=1.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}\).






An eggshell contains 5.0% \(\ce{CaCO3}\) by mass. Ethanoic acid reacts with the carbonate:
\[\ce{CaCO3 + 2CH3COOH -> Ca(CH3COO)2 + H2O + CO2}\]
(a) Calculate the amount of ethanoic acid in \(50.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) solution. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the mass of \(\ce{CaCO3}\) neutralised. [2 marks]
(c) If each eggshell has mass \(50.0\ \mathrm{g}\), calculate the number of eggshells needed. [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(n=cV=2.00\times0.0500=0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\).


(b) Carbonate amount \(=0.100/2=0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\); mass \(=0.0500\times100=5.00\ \mathrm{g}\).


(c) One shell contains \(0.050\times50.0=2.50\ \mathrm{g}\) \(\ce{CaCO3}\), so \(5.00/2.50=2\) shells.






A sample of \(\ce{K2O}\) is dissolved and made up to \(250\ \mathrm{cm^3}\). A \(25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) portion requires \(15.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) sulfuric acid.
\[\ce{K2O + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + H2O}\]
(a) Calculate the amount of sulfuric acid used in the aliquot. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the amount and mass of \(\ce{K2O}\) in the original sample. [4 marks]
(c) Explain why the aliquot volume must be converted to \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) before using \(n=cV\). [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(n=2.00\times0.0150=0.0300\ \mathrm{mol}\).


(b) The equation is 1:1, so the aliquot contains \(0.0300\ \mathrm{mol}\) \(\ce{K2O}\). The full solution contains \(10\times0.0300=0.300\ \mathrm{mol}\); mass \(=0.300\times94.2=28.3\ \mathrm{g}\).


(c) The concentration unit is \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), so the volume must be in \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) for the units to cancel correctly.






A \(1.00\ \mathrm{g}\) ferrochrome sample is dissolved. The iron(II) ions require \(13.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of \(0.100\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) dichromate solution. In the redox reaction, one mole of dichromate reacts with six moles of iron(II).
(a) Calculate the amount of dichromate used. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the amount and mass of iron in the sample. [3 marks]
(c) Calculate the percentage by mass of iron. [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) \(n=0.100\times0.0131=0.00131\ \mathrm{mol}\).


(b) \(n(\ce{Fe^{2+}})=6\times0.00131=0.00786\ \mathrm{mol}\); mass of iron \(=0.00786\times55.8=0.439\ \mathrm{g}\).


(c) Percentage \(=(0.439/1.00)\times100=43.9\%\).

title: 1 Atomic structure
text:
本章对应 CIE 9701 2025–2027 syllabus 的 1.1–1.4 Atomic structure。内容覆盖 subatomic particles、isotopes、electron shells and orbitals，以及 first and successive ionisation energies。


学完本章后，你应该能够：

describe the relative charge, relative mass and location of protons, neutrons and electrons;
use atomic number, nucleon number and ionic charge to calculate numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons;
define isotopes and explain why isotopes have similar chemical properties but slightly different physical properties;
write full electronic configurations and use orbital box notation;
describe the shapes and orientations of s and p orbitals;
define first ionisation energy and write ionisation-energy equations with state symbols;
explain periodic trends and anomalies in first and successive ionisation energies.






An atom contains a small, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons. The nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons; electrons are negatively charged and occupy regions of space described as shells and orbitals.



Subatomic particle
Relative charge
Relative mass
Location




proton
\(+1\)
\(1\)
nucleus


neutron
\(0\)
\(1\)
nucleus


electron
\(-1\)
\(\frac{1}{1836}\)
outside the nucleus






Relative charge and mass of the three subatomic particles


The nucleus is very small compared with the atom, but it contains almost all of the atom’s mass. Most of the volume of an atom is empty space occupied by the electron cloud.



The small dense nucleus and the mainly empty space in an atom





The atomic number, \(Z\), is the number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element. The nucleon number, \(A\), is the total number of protons and neutrons:
\[A = Z + \text{number of neutrons}\]
For a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. For an ion, adjust the number of electrons for the charge:

a \(+1\) ion has one fewer electron than the neutral atom;
a \(2-\) ion has two more electrons than the neutral atom.

Atomic radius generally decreases across a period because nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell. The stronger attraction pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus. Atomic radius increases down a group because an additional occupied shell is added.



Atomic radius trend across a period




Worked example · Note knowledge check


Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in \(^{32}_{15}\mathrm{P}^{3-}\), and state the electronic configuration of the ion.

The atomic number is 15, so there are 15 protons.
\[\text{neutrons}=32-15=17\]
The \(3-\) charge means that three electrons have been gained:
\[\text{electrons}=15+3=18\]
The ion has the same number of electrons as argon:
\[\boxed{1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6}\]








Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They therefore have the same atomic number but different nucleon numbers.



Definition of isotopes


Because isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration, they have the same chemical properties. Their different numbers of neutrons give different masses, so they can have slightly different physical properties such as density, melting point and boiling point.



Examples of isotopes





An ion has a net charge because the number of electrons is different from the number of protons. This is different from an isotope, where the difference is in the number of neutrons.
A free radical is an atom or group of atoms with one or more unpaired electrons. Free radicals are highly reactive. For example, homolytic fission of chlorine under ultraviolet light produces chlorine radicals:
\[\ce{Cl2 ->[UV] 2Cl^.}\]



Ions, isotopes and free radicals





A free radical with an unpaired electron




Worked example · Note definition check


Explain why \(^{35}\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\) have similar chemical properties but different physical properties.

They are isotopes, so they have the same number of protons and the same number of electrons. Their electron configurations are therefore identical, and chemical reactions depend mainly on the outer electrons.
They have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses. This produces small differences in physical properties such as density and boiling point.








Electrons occupy principal energy levels, or shells, numbered \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\). Each shell contains subshells. The subshells used at AS Level are \(s\), \(p\) and, for transition elements, \(d\).

Principal energy levels





Subshells and their capacities


The three p orbitals are oriented at right angles to one another and are labelled \(p_x\), \(p_y\) and \(p_z\).



The three p orbitals





Orientation of the p orbitals





Electrons fill the lowest available energy orbitals first. An orbital can contain a maximum of two electrons, which must have opposite spins. In a set of degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy separate orbitals before pairing.
The usual order for the first few subshells is:
\[1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p\]



Order in which orbitals are filled





Full electronic configurations


For example:
\[\ce{Na}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\]
\[\ce{Cl^-}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\]



Orbital box notation





For transition-metal atoms, the \(4s\) subshell is filled before \(3d\), but the \(4s\) electrons are removed first when positive ions form. For example:
\[\ce{Sc}: [Ar]4s^2 3d^1\]
\[\ce{Sc^{2+}}: [Ar]3d^1\]
The chromium and copper atoms are exceptions to the simple filling pattern because half-filled or completely filled \(3d\) subshells are more stable:
\[\ce{Cr}: [Ar]4s^1 3d^5\]
\[\ce{Cu}: [Ar]4s^1 3d^{10}\]



Transition-metal electron configurations





Electron configurations of ions




Worked example · Note electron configuration


Give the full electronic configurations of \(\ce{K+}\), Ti and Co.

Potassium has atomic number 19. Removing one electron gives:
\[\ce{K+}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\]
Titanium has 22 electrons:
\[\ce{Ti}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,4s^2\,3d^2\]
Cobalt has 27 electrons:
\[\ce{Co}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,4s^2\,3d^7\]








The first ionisation energy is the enthalpy change required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous \(1+\) ions.
The equation for the first ionisation energy of magnesium is:
\[\ce{Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e-}\]
Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron being removed.



Definition of first ionisation energy





First ionisation energy generally increases across a period because:

nuclear charge increases as proton number increases;
electrons are added to the same principal shell, so shielding is similar;
atomic radius decreases and the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron increases.

First ionisation energy generally decreases down a group because the outer electron is in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus, and more shielded by inner electrons. The increase in nuclear charge is outweighed by the greater distance and shielding.



First ionisation energy trend





Successive ionisation energies increase because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion. A large jump shows that the next electron is being removed from an inner shell. The number of electrons removed before the large jump indicates the number of outer-shell electrons and therefore the group.



Successive ionisation energies


The small anomalies across Period 3 are important:

aluminium is lower than magnesium because the electron removed from Al is in the higher-energy, more shielded \(3p\) subshell rather than \(3s\);
sulfur is lower than phosphorus because sulfur has a pair of electrons in one \(3p\) orbital, so electron–electron repulsion makes one electron easier to remove.




Successive ionisation energy pattern





Ionisation-energy anomalies




Worked example · Note ionisation-energy calculation


The successive ionisation energies of an element are 950, 1800, 2700, 4800, 6000 and 12 300 kJ mol\(^{-1}\). Deduce the group of the element and explain your answer.

There is a large jump between the fifth and sixth ionisation energies. The first five electrons are therefore in the outer shell, while the sixth electron is removed from an inner shell.
The element has five outer-shell electrons and is in Group 15 (Group 5 in the older notation).




Worked example · Note periodic trend


Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.

Magnesium loses an electron from the \(3s\) subshell, whereas aluminium loses an electron from the \(3p\) subshell. The \(3p\) electron is at a higher energy and is slightly more shielded, so it is easier to remove. Therefore aluminium has the lower first ionisation energy.

title: 1 Atomic structure
1 Atomic structure
text:
An atom contains a small, dense nucleus surrounded by electrons. The nucleus contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons; electrons are negatively charged and occupy regions of space described as shells and orbitals.



Subatomic particle
Relative charge
Relative mass
Location




proton
\(+1\)
\(1\)
nucleus


neutron
\(0\)
\(1\)
nucleus


electron
\(-1\)
\(\frac{1}{1836}\)
outside the nucleus






Relative charge and mass of the three subatomic particles


The nucleus is very small compared with the atom, but it contains almost all of the atom’s mass. Most of the volume of an atom is empty space occupied by the electron cloud.



The small dense nucleus and the mainly empty space in an atom





The atomic number, \(Z\), is the number of protons in the nucleus. It identifies the element. The nucleon number, \(A\), is the total number of protons and neutrons:
\[A = Z + \text{number of neutrons}\]
For a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. For an ion, adjust the number of electrons for the charge:

a \(+1\) ion has one fewer electron than the neutral atom;
a \(2-\) ion has two more electrons than the neutral atom.

Atomic radius generally decreases across a period because nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell. The stronger attraction pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus. Atomic radius increases down a group because an additional occupied shell is added.



Atomic radius trend across a period




Worked example · Note knowledge check


Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in \(^{32}_{15}\mathrm{P}^{3-}\), and state the electronic configuration of the ion.

The atomic number is 15, so there are 15 protons.
\[\text{neutrons}=32-15=17\]
The \(3-\) charge means that three electrons have been gained:
\[\text{electrons}=15+3=18\]
The ion has the same number of electrons as argon:
\[\boxed{1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6}\]

title: 1 Atomic structure
text:
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They therefore have the same atomic number but different nucleon numbers.



Definition of isotopes


Because isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons and the same electron configuration, they have the same chemical properties. Their different numbers of neutrons give different masses, so they can have slightly different physical properties such as density, melting point and boiling point.



Examples of isotopes





An ion has a net charge because the number of electrons is different from the number of protons. This is different from an isotope, where the difference is in the number of neutrons.
A free radical is an atom or group of atoms with one or more unpaired electrons. Free radicals are highly reactive. For example, homolytic fission of chlorine under ultraviolet light produces chlorine radicals:
\[\ce{Cl2 ->[UV] 2Cl^.}\]



Ions, isotopes and free radicals





A free radical with an unpaired electron




Worked example · Note definition check


Explain why \(^{35}\mathrm{Cl}\) and \(^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\) have similar chemical properties but different physical properties.

They are isotopes, so they have the same number of protons and the same number of electrons. Their electron configurations are therefore identical, and chemical reactions depend mainly on the outer electrons.
They have different numbers of neutrons and therefore different masses. This produces small differences in physical properties such as density and boiling point.

title: 1 Atomic structure
text:
Electrons occupy principal energy levels, or shells, numbered \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\). Each shell contains subshells. The subshells used at AS Level are \(s\), \(p\) and, for transition elements, \(d\).



Subshell
Number of orbitals
Maximum electrons
Shape




\(s\)
1
2
spherical


\(p\)
3
6
three dumbbell-shaped orbitals


\(d\)
5
10
five orbitals






Principal energy levels





Subshells and their capacities


The three p orbitals are oriented at right angles to one another and are labelled \(p_x\), \(p_y\) and \(p_z\).



The three p orbitals





Orientation of the p orbitals





Electrons fill the lowest available energy orbitals first. An orbital can contain a maximum of two electrons, which must have opposite spins. In a set of degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy separate orbitals before pairing.
The usual order for the first few subshells is:
\[1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p\]



Order in which orbitals are filled





Full electronic configurations


For example:
\[\ce{Na}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\]
\[\ce{Cl^-}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\]



Orbital box notation





For transition-metal atoms, the \(4s\) subshell is filled before \(3d\), but the \(4s\) electrons are removed first when positive ions form. For example:
\[\ce{Sc}: [Ar]4s^2 3d^1\]
\[\ce{Sc^{2+}}: [Ar]3d^1\]
The chromium and copper atoms are exceptions to the simple filling pattern because half-filled or completely filled \(3d\) subshells are more stable:
\[\ce{Cr}: [Ar]4s^1 3d^5\]
\[\ce{Cu}: [Ar]4s^1 3d^{10}\]



Transition-metal electron configurations





Electron configurations of ions




Worked example · Note electron configuration


Give the full electronic configurations of \(\ce{K+}\), Ti and Co.

Potassium has atomic number 19. Removing one electron gives:
\[\ce{K+}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\]
Titanium has 22 electrons:
\[\ce{Ti}:1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,4s^2\,3d^2\]
Cobalt has 27 electrons:

title: 1 Atomic structure
text:
The first ionisation energy is the enthalpy change required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous \(1+\) ions.
The equation for the first ionisation energy of magnesium is:
\[\ce{Mg(g) -> Mg+(g) + e-}\]
Ionisation energy is always endothermic because energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the electron being removed.



Definition of first ionisation energy





First ionisation energy generally increases across a period because:

nuclear charge increases as proton number increases;
electrons are added to the same principal shell, so shielding is similar;
atomic radius decreases and the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron increases.

First ionisation energy generally decreases down a group because the outer electron is in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus, and more shielded by inner electrons. The increase in nuclear charge is outweighed by the greater distance and shielding.



First ionisation energy trend





Successive ionisation energies increase because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion. A large jump shows that the next electron is being removed from an inner shell. The number of electrons removed before the large jump indicates the number of outer-shell electrons and therefore the group.



Successive ionisation energies


The small anomalies across Period 3 are important:

aluminium is lower than magnesium because the electron removed from Al is in the higher-energy, more shielded \(3p\) subshell rather than \(3s\);
sulfur is lower than phosphorus because sulfur has a pair of electrons in one \(3p\) orbital, so electron–electron repulsion makes one electron easier to remove.




Successive ionisation energy pattern





Ionisation-energy anomalies




Worked example · Note ionisation-energy calculation


The successive ionisation energies of an element are 950, 1800, 2700, 4800, 6000 and 12 300 kJ mol\(^{-1}\). Deduce the group of the element and explain your answer.

There is a large jump between the fifth and sixth ionisation energies. The first five electrons are therefore in the outer shell, while the sixth electron is removed from an inner shell.
The element has five outer-shell electrons and is in Group 15 (Group 5 in the older notation).




Worked example · Note periodic trend


Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.

Magnesium loses an electron from the \(3s\) subshell, whereas aluminium loses an electron from the \(3p\) subshell. The \(3p\) electron is at a higher energy and is slightly more shielded, so it is easier to remove. Therefore aluminium has the lower first ionisation energy.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
本章对应 CIE 9701 AS Chemistry 的 Chemical bonding。内容覆盖 electronegativity、ionic bonding、metallic bonding、covalent and coordinate bonding、shapes of molecules、intermolecular forces、bond properties 以及 dot-and-cross diagrams。


学完本章后，你应该能够：

define electronegativity and explain trends across a period and down a group;
describe ionic, metallic, covalent and coordinate bonding;
explain how bonding and structure determine physical properties;
draw dot-and-cross diagrams for atoms, ions, molecules and polyatomic ions;
use electron-pair repulsion to predict molecular shapes and bond angles;
distinguish sigma and pi bonds;
explain London dispersion forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonding;
relate bond polarity, bond length and bond energy to electronegativity and atomic size.





Bonding explains structure; structure explains melting point, conductivity, solubility and mechanical properties.
A polar bond does not guarantee a polar molecule: draw the shape and decide whether bond dipoles cancel.
A covalent bond is an intramolecular bond; London forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonds are intermolecular attractions.
In an ionic lattice, greater ionic charge and smaller ionic radius generally give stronger electrostatic attraction.






Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
Across a period, electronegativity generally increases because nuclear charge increases while the bonding electrons remain in the same principal shell. Atomic radius decreases and the attraction for the bonding pair becomes stronger.
Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases because the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more inner shells shield the nuclear charge.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element in the usual CIE scale. The noble gases are normally omitted because they do not commonly form covalent bonds in the AS syllabus.



If two bonded atoms have different electronegativities, the bonding electrons are attracted more strongly to one atom. The more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, \(\delta-\), and the other atom carries a partial positive charge, \(\delta+\).
The C–H bond is treated as approximately non-polar at this level. C–O, C–F and C–Cl bonds are polar with the carbon atom as \(\delta+\) and the more electronegative atom as \(\delta-\).
Bond polarity is not the same as molecular polarity. A molecule can contain polar bonds but have no overall dipole if the bond dipoles cancel because of its symmetrical shape, as in \(\ce{CO2}\).

To decide molecular polarity, use this order: identify polar bonds, draw the 3-D shape, then add the bond dipoles as vectors. CO2, BF3 and CCl4 are symmetrical and non-polar overall; H2O, NH3 and CH2Cl2 have a net dipole.





An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. A metal atom forms a positive ion by losing one or more outer-shell electrons; a non-metal atom forms a negative ion by gaining electrons.
The ions arrange themselves in a giant three-dimensional lattice. Each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions, so the attraction acts in all directions. The formula of an ionic compound gives the simplest whole-number ratio of ions that makes the compound electrically neutral.
Examples:



Ions
Formula




\(\ce{Na+}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\)
\(\ce{NaCl}\)


\(\ce{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\)
\(\ce{MgCl2}\)


\(\ce{Al^{3+}}\) and \(\ce{O^{2-}}\)
\(\ce{Al2O3}\)


\(\ce{Ca^{2+}}\) and \(\ce{PO4^{3-}}\)
\(\ce{Ca3(PO4)2}\)






Ionic compounds usually have high melting and boiling points because many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome.
They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are fixed in position. They conduct when molten or dissolved in water because the ions are then mobile.
An ionic crystal is brittle. When a layer shifts, ions of the same charge can become adjacent and repel strongly, causing the crystal to split.

For a comparison of melting points, state both factors: attraction is stronger when ion charges are larger and when ionic radii are smaller, because oppositely charged ions are closer together. This explains why MgO has much stronger ionic bonding and a higher melting point than NaCl.





Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons. The outer electrons are not associated with one particular atom and can move through the structure.
Metals conduct electricity because delocalised electrons carry charge. They conduct heat because mobile electrons transfer energy rapidly through the lattice.
Metallic bonding is non-directional. Layers of metal ions can slide while the attraction to the delocalised electrons remains, so metals are malleable and ductile.



An alloy contains atoms of different elements. The different-sized atoms distort the layers of the metal lattice and make it more difficult for the layers to slide. Alloys are therefore usually harder than pure metals.
Increasing the number of delocalised electrons or increasing the charge density of the metal ions generally strengthens metallic bonding, although the exact properties depend on the alloy structure.






A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms. A single covalent bond contains one shared pair; a double bond contains two shared pairs and a triple bond contains three shared pairs.
The shared pair is formed by overlap of atomic orbitals. A sigma (\(\sigma\)) bond is formed by end-on overlap along the line joining the nuclei. A pi (\(\pi\)) bond is formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals and has electron density above and below the internuclear axis.
A double bond contains one \(\sigma\) bond and one \(\pi\) bond. A triple bond contains one \(\sigma\) bond and two \(\pi\) bonds.



A coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom. The donor must have a lone pair and the acceptor must have an empty orbital or be electron-deficient.
Examples include:
\[\ce{NH3 + H+ -> NH4+}\]
\[\ce{H2O + H+ -> H3O+}\]
The bond is represented by an arrow from the donor atom to the acceptor atom. Once formed, a coordinate bond behaves like an ordinary covalent bond.



A shorter covalent bond is generally stronger and has a greater bond energy. Between the same two elements, bond length decreases and bond energy increases in the order single bond < double bond < triple bond.
Down a group, larger atoms usually form longer, weaker bonds because the bonding pair is further from the nuclei. A large electronegativity difference increases bond polarity but does not by itself mean that a bond is fully ionic.






Electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs because their electron density is concentrated closer to the central atom.
The repulsion order is:
\[\text{lone pair--lone pair} > \text{lone pair--bond pair} > \text{bond pair--bond pair}\]
Multiple bonds are treated as one region of electron density, but they repel slightly more strongly than a single bond.

Examples include \(\ce{CO2}\) linear, \(\ce{BF3}\) trigonal planar, \(\ce{CH4}\) tetrahedral, \(\ce{NH3}\) trigonal pyramidal and \(\ce{H2O}\) bent.
The shape is named from the positions of bonded atoms, not lone pairs. For example NH3 has four electron regions but is trigonal pyramidal, while H2O has four electron regions but is bent. In PCl5, three bonds are equatorial (120°) and two are axial (90° to the equatorial bonds); in SF6 all adjacent bonds are 90°.





London dispersion forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron density. A temporary dipole can induce a dipole in a neighbouring particle.
They act between all atoms and molecules. They become stronger when there are more electrons and a larger, more easily polarised electron cloud. Long molecules can also have stronger dispersion forces because they have a larger contact surface.



Polar molecules have permanent partial charges. The \(\delta+\) end of one molecule attracts the \(\delta-\) end of another. Permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces are stronger than dispersion forces for molecules of similar size.
The overall dipole depends on both bond polarity and molecular shape. The polar bonds in \(\ce{CO2}\) cancel, whereas the polar bonds in \(\ce{H2O}\) do not.



Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong permanent dipole attraction. It occurs when hydrogen is covalently bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in a neighbouring molecule.
Hydrogen bonding explains the relatively high boiling point of water and the high solubility of small alcohols and ammonia in water. It also contributes to the high surface tension of water.

Hydrogen bonding requires H directly bonded to N, O or F. It is not caused merely by the presence of hydrogen in a molecule; CH4 cannot hydrogen bond. When comparing boiling points, first compare molecular size/London forces, then polarity, then check for hydrogen bonding.


Boiling a molecular substance involves overcoming intermolecular forces, not breaking the covalent bonds inside each molecule. Larger molecules often have higher boiling points because their dispersion forces are stronger.
For molecules with similar size, a polar molecule generally has a higher boiling point than a non-polar molecule. Hydrogen bonding usually gives the largest increase among the intermolecular forces in this syllabus.

Put brackets around a polyatomic ion and write its charge outside the bracket.

In a dot-and-cross diagram, dots and crosses distinguish electrons contributed by different atoms. A shared pair must contain two electrons, while a lone pair remains on one atom.


Worked example · Ammonium ion


Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen. The hydrogen ion has no electrons. The lone pair is donated to \(\ce{H+}\) to form a coordinate bond, giving four N–H bonds and an overall \(1+\) charge.
The nitrogen atom has no lone pair remaining in \(\ce{NH4+}\), and the ion is drawn in square brackets with the charge outside.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
3 Chemical bonding
text:
Bonding explains structure; structure explains melting point, conductivity, solubility and mechanical properties.
A polar bond does not guarantee a polar molecule: draw the shape and decide whether bond dipoles cancel.
A covalent bond is an intramolecular bond; London forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonds are intermolecular attractions.
In an ionic lattice, greater ionic charge and smaller ionic radius generally give stronger electrostatic attraction.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
Across a period, electronegativity generally increases because nuclear charge increases while the bonding electrons remain in the same principal shell. Atomic radius decreases and the attraction for the bonding pair becomes stronger.
Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases because the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more inner shells shield the nuclear charge.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element in the usual CIE scale. The noble gases are normally omitted because they do not commonly form covalent bonds in the AS syllabus.



If two bonded atoms have different electronegativities, the bonding electrons are attracted more strongly to one atom. The more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, \(\delta-\), and the other atom carries a partial positive charge, \(\delta+\).
The C–H bond is treated as approximately non-polar at this level. C–O, C–F and C–Cl bonds are polar with the carbon atom as \(\delta+\) and the more electronegative atom as \(\delta-\).
Bond polarity is not the same as molecular polarity. A molecule can contain polar bonds but have no overall dipole if the bond dipoles cancel because of its symmetrical shape, as in \(\ce{CO2}\).

To decide molecular polarity, use this order: identify polar bonds, draw the 3-D shape, then add the bond dipoles as vectors. CO2, BF3 and CCl4 are symmetrical and non-polar overall; H2O, NH3 and CH2Cl2 have a net dipole.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. A metal atom forms a positive ion by losing one or more outer-shell electrons; a non-metal atom forms a negative ion by gaining electrons.
The ions arrange themselves in a giant three-dimensional lattice. Each ion is surrounded by oppositely charged ions, so the attraction acts in all directions. The formula of an ionic compound gives the simplest whole-number ratio of ions that makes the compound electrically neutral.
Examples:



Ions
Formula




\(\ce{Na+}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\)
\(\ce{NaCl}\)


\(\ce{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\)
\(\ce{MgCl2}\)


\(\ce{Al^{3+}}\) and \(\ce{O^{2-}}\)
\(\ce{Al2O3}\)


\(\ce{Ca^{2+}}\) and \(\ce{PO4^{3-}}\)
\(\ce{Ca3(PO4)2}\)






Ionic compounds usually have high melting and boiling points because many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome.
They do not conduct electricity when solid because the ions are fixed in position. They conduct when molten or dissolved in water because the ions are then mobile.
An ionic crystal is brittle. When a layer shifts, ions of the same charge can become adjacent and repel strongly, causing the crystal to split.

For a comparison of melting points, state both factors: attraction is stronger when ion charges are larger and when ionic radii are smaller, because oppositely charged ions are closer together. This explains why MgO has much stronger ionic bonding and a higher melting point than NaCl.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
Metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons. The outer electrons are not associated with one particular atom and can move through the structure.
Metals conduct electricity because delocalised electrons carry charge. They conduct heat because mobile electrons transfer energy rapidly through the lattice.
Metallic bonding is non-directional. Layers of metal ions can slide while the attraction to the delocalised electrons remains, so metals are malleable and ductile.



An alloy contains atoms of different elements. The different-sized atoms distort the layers of the metal lattice and make it more difficult for the layers to slide. Alloys are therefore usually harder than pure metals.
Increasing the number of delocalised electrons or increasing the charge density of the metal ions generally strengthens metallic bonding, although the exact properties depend on the alloy structure.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms. A single covalent bond contains one shared pair; a double bond contains two shared pairs and a triple bond contains three shared pairs.
The shared pair is formed by overlap of atomic orbitals. A sigma (\(\sigma\)) bond is formed by end-on overlap along the line joining the nuclei. A pi (\(\pi\)) bond is formed by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals and has electron density above and below the internuclear axis.
A double bond contains one \(\sigma\) bond and one \(\pi\) bond. A triple bond contains one \(\sigma\) bond and two \(\pi\) bonds.



A coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom. The donor must have a lone pair and the acceptor must have an empty orbital or be electron-deficient.
Examples include:
\[\ce{NH3 + H+ -> NH4+}\]
\[\ce{H2O + H+ -> H3O+}\]
The bond is represented by an arrow from the donor atom to the acceptor atom. Once formed, a coordinate bond behaves like an ordinary covalent bond.



A shorter covalent bond is generally stronger and has a greater bond energy. Between the same two elements, bond length decreases and bond energy increases in the order single bond < double bond < triple bond.
Down a group, larger atoms usually form longer, weaker bonds because the bonding pair is further from the nuclei. A large electronegativity difference increases bond polarity but does not by itself mean that a bond is fully ionic.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
Electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs because their electron density is concentrated closer to the central atom.
The repulsion order is:
\[\text{lone pair--lone pair} > \text{lone pair--bond pair} > \text{bond pair--bond pair}\]
Multiple bonds are treated as one region of electron density, but they repel slightly more strongly than a single bond.

octahedral
\(90^\circ\)



Examples include \(\ce{CO2}\) linear, \(\ce{BF3}\) trigonal planar, \(\ce{CH4}\) tetrahedral, \(\ce{NH3}\) trigonal pyramidal and \(\ce{H2O}\) bent.
The shape is named from the positions of bonded atoms, not lone pairs. For example NH3 has four electron regions but is trigonal pyramidal, while H2O has four electron regions but is bent. In PCl5, three bonds are equatorial (120°) and two are axial (90° to the equatorial bonds); in SF6 all adjacent bonds are 90°.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
London dispersion forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron density. A temporary dipole can induce a dipole in a neighbouring particle.
They act between all atoms and molecules. They become stronger when there are more electrons and a larger, more easily polarised electron cloud. Long molecules can also have stronger dispersion forces because they have a larger contact surface.



Polar molecules have permanent partial charges. The \(\delta+\) end of one molecule attracts the \(\delta-\) end of another. Permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces are stronger than dispersion forces for molecules of similar size.
The overall dipole depends on both bond polarity and molecular shape. The polar bonds in \(\ce{CO2}\) cancel, whereas the polar bonds in \(\ce{H2O}\) do not.



Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong permanent dipole attraction. It occurs when hydrogen is covalently bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in a neighbouring molecule.
Hydrogen bonding explains the relatively high boiling point of water and the high solubility of small alcohols and ammonia in water. It also contributes to the high surface tension of water.

Hydrogen bonding requires H directly bonded to N, O or F. It is not caused merely by the presence of hydrogen in a molecule; CH4 cannot hydrogen bond. When comparing boiling points, first compare molecular size/London forces, then polarity, then check for hydrogen bonding.


Boiling a molecular substance involves overcoming intermolecular forces, not breaking the covalent bonds inside each molecule. Larger molecules often have higher boiling points because their dispersion forces are stronger.
For molecules with similar size, a polar molecule generally has a higher boiling point than a non-polar molecule. Hydrogen bonding usually gives the largest increase among the intermolecular forces in this syllabus.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
Count the total valence electrons, adjusting for the charge of an ion.
Choose a central atom; hydrogen is never central and the least electronegative suitable atom is usually central.
Add single bonds and complete the outer atoms’ octets.
Place remaining electrons on the central atom.
If the central atom lacks an octet, form multiple bonds where appropriate.
Put brackets around a polyatomic ion and write its charge outside the bracket.

In a dot-and-cross diagram, dots and crosses distinguish electrons contributed by different atoms. A shared pair must contain two electrons, while a lone pair remains on one atom.


Worked example · Ammonium ion


Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen. The hydrogen ion has no electrons. The lone pair is donated to \(\ce{H+}\) to form a coordinate bond, giving four N–H bonds and an overall \(1+\) charge.
The nitrogen atom has no lone pair remaining in \(\ce{NH4+}\), and the ion is drawn in square brackets with the charge outside.

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
Phosphine, \(\ce{PH3}\), reacts with a hydrogen ion to form \(\ce{PH4+}\). Which type of bond is formed between P and H in this reaction?


AHydrogen bond


BCoordinate covalent bond


CIonic bond


DMetallic bond



Check answer





Show explanation


B. The lone pair on phosphorus is donated to the electron-deficient \(\ce{H+}\) ion.







Which forces act between neighbouring iodine molecules in solid iodine and between particles in solid silver?


AMetallic bonds; covalent bonds


BIonic bonds; metallic bonds


CCovalent bonds; covalent bonds


DLondon dispersion forces; metallic bonds



Check answer





Show explanation


D. \(\ce{I2}\) molecules are held together by London forces; silver has a lattice of metal ions and delocalised electrons.







Which solid contains more than one type of bonding?


ADiamond


BSodium chloride


CIron


DIce



Check answer





Show explanation


D. Ice contains covalent bonds within water molecules and hydrogen bonds between molecules.







What is the shape around each nitrogen atom in hydrazine, \(\ce{N2H4}\)?


ATrigonal planar, \(120^\circ\)


BTrigonal pyramidal, about \(107^\circ\)


CLinear, \(180^\circ\)


DSquare planar, \(90^\circ\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Each N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. Lone-pair repulsion reduces the tetrahedral angle to about \(107^\circ\).







Which bond polarity assignment is not correct?


A\(\ce{C^{\delta+}-O^{\delta-}}\) in propanol


B\(\ce{C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}}\) in propanal


C\(\ce{C^{\delta+}-H^{\delta-}}\) in propane


D\(\ce{C^{\delta+}-Cl^{\delta-}}\) in chloropropane



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Carbon is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen, so the C–H bond is treated as approximately non-polar rather than with H as \(\delta-\).







Which statement correctly describes the formation of \(\ce{NH4+}\) from \(\ce{NH3}\) and \(\ce{H+}\)?


AHydrogen donates one electron to nitrogen.


BNitrogen donates its lone pair to hydrogen.


CFour electrons are transferred from nitrogen to hydrogen.


DThe hydrogen ion supplies a lone pair.



Check answer





Show explanation


B. The N lone pair forms the fourth N–H coordinate bond.







What are the shapes around boron in \(\ce{BF3}\) and \(\ce{BH4-}\)?


APyramidal; tetrahedral


BPyramidal; square planar


CTrigonal planar; tetrahedral


DTrigonal planar; square planar



Check answer





Show explanation


C. \(\ce{BF3}\) has three bonding pairs; \(\ce{BH4-}\) has four.







Which atom is most electronegative?


ACl


BMg


CBr


DNa



Check answer





Show explanation


A. Electronegativity decreases down Group 17, so chlorine is more electronegative than bromine.







Which compound is not an ionic compound?


A\(\ce{CaCO3}\)


B\(\ce{CH3OH}\)


C\(\ce{NaOH}\)


D\(\ce{BaCl2}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Methanol is a molecular covalent substance. The other compounds contain ions, even though carbonate or hydroxide also contain covalent bonds internally.







Which statement describes metallic bonding?


AAttraction between oppositely charged ions


BAttraction between permanent molecular dipoles


CAttraction between shared pairs and two nuclei only


DAttraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons



Check answer





Show explanation


D. This is the definition of metallic bonding.







Which material contains only one main type of bonding in its solid structure?


AGraphite


BBrass


CIce


DIodine crystals



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Brass is an alloy with metallic bonding. Graphite, ice and iodine have bonding within particles plus intermolecular attractions.







What happens when \(\ce{SiCl4}\) is added to water?


AIt reacts to give only an acidic solution.


BIt reacts to give a precipitate and an acidic solution.


CIt reacts to give a precipitate and a neutral solution.


DIt dissolves to give only a neutral solution.



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Hydrolysis forms solid \(\ce{SiO2}\) and hydrochloric acid.










For \(\ce{PCl5(g) <=> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g)}\), the percentage yield of \(\ce{PCl3}\) increases from 13% at \(160^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to 100% at \(300^\circ\mathrm{C}\). What is correct?


AThe reaction is exothermic; \(\ce{PCl3}\) is pyramidal.


BThe reaction is exothermic; \(\ce{PCl3}\) is trigonal planar.


CThe reaction is endothermic; \(\ce{PCl3}\) is pyramidal.


DThe reaction is endothermic; \(\ce{PCl3}\) is trigonal planar.



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Higher temperature favours the endothermic forward reaction. \(\ce{PCl3}\) has three bonds and one lone pair, giving a pyramidal shape.







Which feature is not present in a nitrogen molecule, \(\ce{N2}\)?


ATwo lone pairs in total


BThree shared electron pairs


CThree \(\pi\) bonds


DA bond angle of \(180^\circ\)



Check answer





Show explanation


C. A triple bond contains one \(\sigma\) bond and two \(\pi\) bonds.







Which ion has three lone pairs around its central atom?


A\(\ce{PF6-}\)


B\(\ce{ClF2-}\)


C\(\ce{BF4-}\)


D\(\ce{SF6}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. In \(\ce{ClF2-}\), chlorine has two bonding pairs and three lone pairs.







Which change of state involves overcoming only London dispersion forces?


A\(\ce{C3H6(l) -> C3H6(s)}\)


B\(\ce{CO2(l) -> CO2(g)}\)


C\(\ce{H2O(s) -> H2O(l)}\)


D\(\ce{C2H5OH(l) -> C2H5OH(g)}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Carbon dioxide is non-polar and has no permanent dipole or hydrogen bonding.







What is the formula of the cyanate ion in ammonium cyanate?


A\(\ce{CO-}\)


B\(\ce{NO-}\)


C\(\ce{CNO-}\)


D\(\ce{CNO2-}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Ammonium cyanate is \(\ce{NH4OCN}\) and contains the cyanate ion \(\ce{OCN-}\), written here as \(\ce{CNO-}\).







Which pair of words does not correctly complete the statement: “The bond ___ between H and the halogen in HBr is ___ than in HI”?


Alength; shorter


Benergy; greater


Cangle; smaller


Dpolarity; greater



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Hydrogen halides are diatomic, so a bond angle is not defined.







How many \(\sigma\) and \(\pi\) bonds are in ethene, \(\ce{C2H4}\)?


A4 \(\sigma\), 1 \(\pi\)


B5 \(\sigma\), 1 \(\pi\)


C5 \(\sigma\), 2 \(\pi\)


D6 \(\sigma\), 1 \(\pi\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. There are four C–H \(\sigma\) bonds and one C–C \(\sigma\) bond, plus one C–C \(\pi\) bond.










Hydrogen bonding occurs between liquid methanal, \(\ce{HCHO}\), and a second liquid \(Y\). Which substance is most likely to be \(Y\)?


A\(\ce{CH3CO2CH3}\)


B\(\ce{CH3OH}\)


C\(\ce{CH3COCH3}\)


D\(\ce{CH3CHO}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


B. Methanol has an O–H hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen lone pairs; the carbonyl oxygen of methanal can accept the hydrogen bond.







Why does the rate of hydrolysis of \(\ce{R-Cl}\), \(\ce{R-Br}\) and \(\ce{R-I}\) generally increase from chlorine to iodine?


AThe first ionisation energy of the halogen increases.


BThe silver halide solubility increases from chloride to iodide.


CThe R–X bond energy decreases from R–Cl to R–I.


DThe R–X bond polarity increases from R–Cl to R–I.



Check answer





Show explanation


C. The larger iodine atom forms a longer, weaker R–I bond that breaks more readily.







Which atom is most likely to form a covalent bond with fluorine rather than an ionic bond, based on the smallest electronegativity difference?


AH, \(\chi=2.20\)


BCu, \(\chi=1.95\)


CMg, \(\chi=1.30\)


DK, \(\chi=0.82\)



Check answer





Show explanation


A. Hydrogen has the closest electronegativity to fluorine among the options, so the H–F bond is covalent and strongly polar.







Which description of dipoles in \(\ce{CHCl3}\) and \(\ce{Br2}\) is correct?


AInduced only in both molecules


BInduced only in \(\ce{CHCl3}\); induced and permanent in \(\ce{Br2}\)


CInduced and permanent in both


DInduced and permanent in \(\ce{CHCl3}\); induced only in \(\ce{Br2}\)



Check answer





Show explanation


D. \(\ce{CHCl3}\) is polar, while symmetrical \(\ce{Br2}\) is non-polar but still has temporary dipoles.







Hydroxyapatite contains calcium, hydroxide and phosphate ions. Which statement is correct?


AIt contains only metallic bonding.


BStrontium forms covalent bonds with phosphate ions.


CStrontium ions are similar enough in size to replace calcium ions in the lattice.


DPhosphate ions are held together by metallic bonding.



Check answer





Show explanation


C. Similar-sized ions can occupy similar lattice sites; the bonding between calcium/strontium ions and anions is ionic.







Which substance is expected to have a high melting point and conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?


AA giant ionic compound


BA simple molecular compound


CA noble gas


DA molecular non-polar liquid



Check answer





Show explanation


A. Strong ionic attractions give a high melting point; mobile ions in the molten state carry charge.







What is the shape of \(\ce{PF6-}\)?


ATetrahedral


BTrigonal pyramidal


CTrigonal bipyramidal


DOctahedral



Check answer





Show explanation


D. Six bonding pairs around phosphorus repel to an octahedral arrangement.







Which feature disappears when \(\ce{C2H4}\) is converted to \(\ce{C2H6}\) by hydrogenation?


AThe C–C \(\sigma\) bond


BThe C–C \(\pi\) bond


CAll C–H \(\sigma\) bonds


DAll electron pairs on carbon

Show explanation


B. Hydrogen adds across the double bond, converting the \(\pi\) component into two new C–H bonds.







Which molecule has the largest overall dipole?


A\(\ce{CCl4}\)


B\(\ce{CH2Cl2}\)


C\(\ce{BF3}\)


D\(\ce{CO2}\)

title: 3 Chemical bonding
text:
(a) Name the three main types of intermolecular force and arrange them in increasing order of strength. [2 marks]
(b) Methanol, \(\ce{CH3OH}\), is a small polar molecule. Describe how two methanol molecules form a hydrogen bond. Include the partial charges and the lone pair involved. [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) London dispersion forces, permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces, hydrogen bonds, in that order.


(b) Oxygen is \(\delta-\) and the O–H hydrogen is \(\delta+\). The \(\delta+\) hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. A hydrogen bond is shown as a dashed line.






Ammonia is very soluble in water.
(a) State why ammonia is polar. [2 marks]
(b) Describe two possible hydrogen bonds between one water molecule and one ammonia molecule. [4 marks]
(c) State one physical property of ammonia caused by its polarity. [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) N–H bonds are polar and the molecule is trigonal pyramidal, so the bond dipoles do not cancel.


(b) A water \(\delta+\) H can hydrogen-bond to the lone pair on N; an ammonia \(\delta+\) H can hydrogen-bond to a lone pair on O. Partial charges and the dashed attractions must be shown correctly.


(c) It is soluble in water, or has a higher boiling point than a similar non-polar molecule.






Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for \(\ce{H2}\), \(\ce{Cl2}\) and \(\ce{HCl}\).
(a) Show the bonding pair and all lone pairs. [3 marks]
(b) Explain why the H–Cl bond is polar. [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Each molecule must have one shared pair. \(\ce{H2}\) has no lone pairs; each chlorine in \(\ce{Cl2}\) has three lone pairs; chlorine in \(\ce{HCl}\) has three lone pairs.


(b) Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the bonding pair is closer to chlorine, giving \(\ce{H^{\delta+}-Cl^{\delta-}}\).






For each species, state the number of bonding pairs, number of lone pairs on the central atom, shape and approximate bond angle: \(\ce{CO2}\), \(\ce{BF3}\), \(\ce{CH4}\), \(\ce{NH3}\) and \(\ce{H2O}\). [10 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



\(\ce{CO2}\): 2 regions, 0 lone pairs, linear, \(180^\circ\).


\(\ce{BF3}\): 3 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs, trigonal planar, \(120^\circ\).


\(\ce{CH4}\): 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs, tetrahedral, \(109.5^\circ\).


\(\ce{NH3}\): 3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair, trigonal pyramidal, about \(107^\circ\).


\(\ce{H2O}\): 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs, bent, about \(104.5^\circ\).






Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice.
(a) Describe the structure of solid sodium chloride. [2 marks]
(b) Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does. [2 marks]
(c) Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point. [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) A regular three-dimensional lattice of oppositely charged \(\ce{Na+}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\) ions; each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.


(b) Solid ions are fixed, whereas molten ions are mobile and can carry charge.


(c) Strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions require much energy to overcome.









The equilibrium is:
\[\ce{PCl5(g) <=> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g)}\]
The yield of \(\ce{PCl3}\) increases as temperature increases.
(a) State whether the forward reaction is endothermic or exothermic and explain. [2 marks]
(b) State the shape and bond angle around phosphorus in \(\ce{PCl3}\). [2 marks]
(c) Explain why the bond angle is less than \(109.5^\circ\). [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Endothermic; increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction and increases the product yield.


(b) Trigonal pyramidal; approximately \(107^\circ\).


(c) There are three bonding pairs and one lone pair. Lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion is stronger than bond-pair–bond-pair repulsion and compresses the angle.






(a) Explain the meaning of bond polarity using ammonia as an example. [2 marks]
(b) Explain why the ammonia molecule is polar. [1 mark]
(c) State one physical property of ammonia caused by its polarity. [1 mark]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electron pair in each N–H bond is displaced towards N, giving partial charges.


(b) Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, so the three N–H bond dipoles do not cancel.


(c) High solubility in water, or a relatively high boiling point compared with a similar non-polar molecule.






When ammonia gas reacts with hydrogen chloride, solid ammonium chloride forms.
(a) State the types of bond present within one formula unit of \(\ce{NH4Cl}\). [3 marks]
(b) State how many of each bond type are present if the coordinate bond is shown separately. [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Ionic attraction between \(\ce{NH4+}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\); covalent N–H bonds within ammonium; one of the N–H bonds is coordinate.


(b) One ionic attraction type, four N–H covalent bonds in the ammonium ion, with one formed originally as a coordinate bond. The coordinate bond is chemically equivalent to the other N–H bonds after formation.






A paperclip can float on water, but sinks after a small amount of soap is added.
Explain both observations in terms of intermolecular forces. [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer


Water has high surface tension caused by hydrogen bonding between water molecules. The surface can support the paperclip if it is placed carefully. Soap disrupts the hydrogen-bond network and lowers surface tension, so the paperclip sinks.





Compare the boiling points of \(\ce{F2}\) and \(\ce{HCl}\).
(a) Identify the intermolecular forces present in each substance. [2 marks]
(b) Predict which has the lower boiling point. [1 mark]
(c) Explain the difference. [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Both have London dispersion forces; HCl also has permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces.


(b) \(\ce{F2}\) has the lower boiling point.


(c) HCl has stronger intermolecular attractions because it is polar, so more energy is required to separate its molecules.









The nitrate ion is \(\ce{NO3-}\).
(a) Calculate the total number of valence electrons in one nitrate ion. [2 marks]
(b) Describe how the electrons are arranged in a valid dot-and-cross structure. [3 marks]
(c) Explain why the three N–O bonds are equivalent in the real ion. [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) N contributes 5, three O atoms contribute 18 and the negative charge contributes one: total 24 electrons.


(b) N is central, three O atoms are attached, the ion is placed in square brackets with a \(1-\) charge, and the octet/charge arrangement is shown correctly. Equivalent resonance structures can be drawn with the double bond in different positions.


(c) The actual ion is a resonance hybrid; the bonding electrons are delocalised over all three N–O bonds.






Methanamide has formula \(\ce{HCONH2}\).
(a) State the shape and approximate bond angle around the carbon atom. [2 marks]
(b) State the shape and approximate bond angle around the nitrogen atom. [2 marks]
(c) Explain why the two shapes are different. [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) The carbonyl carbon has three regions of electron density, so it is trigonal planar, about \(120^\circ\).


(b) Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, so it is trigonal pyramidal, about \(107^\circ\).


(c) The nitrogen lone pair gives four electron regions and stronger lone-pair repulsion; the carbon atom has three regions and no lone pair.






(a) Explain how \(\ce{PCl6-}\) can form from \(\ce{PCl5}\) and \(\ce{Cl-}\). [3 marks]
(b) State the shape of \(\ce{PCl6-}\) and justify it using electron-pair repulsion. [2 marks]
(c) Explain why nitrogen cannot form \(\ce{NCl5}\). [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) A lone pair on \(\ce{Cl-}\) is donated to electron-deficient P, forming a coordinate P–Cl bond and the ion \(\ce{PCl6-}\).


(b) Octahedral; six bonding pairs repel equally and occupy positions as far apart as possible.


(c) Nitrogen is a Period 2 atom with no available d orbitals and cannot expand its octet beyond eight electrons.






Water and ammonia can form hydrogen bonds with each other.
(a) Draw or describe the partial charges on \(\ce{H2O}\) and \(\ce{NH3}\). [2 marks]
(b) Describe both possible directions of hydrogen bonding between the two molecules. [4 marks]
(c) Explain why these interactions make ammonia highly soluble in water. [2 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) O and N are \(\delta-\); bonded H atoms are \(\delta+\).


(b) Water H can donate a hydrogen bond to the lone pair on N. Ammonia H can donate a hydrogen bond to a lone pair on O. Both attractions should be shown with dashed lines.


(c) Strong attractions form between ammonia and water molecules, replacing some water–water and ammonia–ammonia attractions and allowing the molecules to mix.






Solid phosphorus(V) chloride has a higher melting point than liquid antimony(V) chloride.
(a) State the particles and bonding in solid \(\ce{PCl5}\). [2 marks]
(b) State the particles and intermolecular forces in liquid \(\ce{SbCl5}\). [2 marks]
(c) Explain the difference in melting points. [3 marks]


Show mark scheme / model answer



(a) Solid \(\ce{PCl5}\) contains \(\ce{PCl4+}\) and \(\ce{PCl6-}\) ions in a giant ionic lattice with strong ionic attractions.


(b) Liquid \(\ce{SbCl5}\) contains covalent molecules held together by relatively weak intermolecular forces.


(c) More energy is needed to overcome strong ionic attractions in solid \(\ce{PCl5}\) than weak intermolecular forces between \(\ce{SbCl5}\) molecules.
